newsitem.title: UK: Environment groups criticise UK road strategy.
newsitem.headline: Environment groups criticise UK road strategy.

text.p: The Department of Transport launched an environmental five year plan for Britain's roads on Wednesday, covering issues from pollution to protection of owls breeding but the plan drew criticism from the "green' lobby.
John Watts, minister for railways, roads and local transport unveiled the government's first environmental strategy for the English road network on Wednesday.

He said the strategy, allocated a 13 million pounds research budget, was launched by the government's Highways Agency. Research will cover issues including the relationship of roads and verges to the bird population.
Other tasks will be to establish trees where roads dominate, examine air quality and techniques which allow less salt to be spread on roads.
But a spokeswoman from pressure group Transport 2000, one of the groups advising the DOT when it was forming its strategy, attacked it as no more than a "series of surface measures."
"What is the point in gouging out great swathes of the British countrywide and then planting a few shrubs in return?" said Emma Must of Transport 2000.

She said green groups had made it clear only "non-road building options" would work, together with greater spending on road maintenance and efforts to encourage use of public transport and cheaper green fuel.
The London Ecology Centre's spokeswoman said the proposals were "a cosmetic exercise."

But Watts noted at the opening of a southern by-pass for Bedford, north of London, that particular route had bought benefits. "Two wetland areas have been created and altogether 110,000 trees and shrubs will be planted...to help blend the new road into the landscape and provide valuable habitats for wildlife."
